Directions: Exit the parking lot by making a right on Cold Harbor Road
(Route 156). After traveling 4.1 miles on Cold Harbor Road, turn left on
Old Hanover Road. Go for 0.2 mile on Old Hanover Road and then turn
left on Grapevine Road. After 1.4 miles, turn left on Meadow Road. After
2.6 miles on Meadow Road, you will come to an intersection with US
Highway 60. (The intersection of Meadow Road and US Highway 60 is
a good place to stop for lunch, because fast food and convenience stores
are nearby.) Continue on Meadow Road for 5.0 miles. Along the way,
Meadow Road will change its name to Elko Road. After 5 miles, turn
right on Charles City Road. Travel on Charles City Road for 1.2 miles
where you will reach a four-way intersection. At this intersection, Charles
City Road comes from the east and then turns right (north). If you were to
continue straight, the road becomes Darbytown Road. The road to the left
(south) is Willis Church Road. The stand is at this intersection. It is best
to turn right where there is some room on the right side of the road to park
and exit the vehicles for the stand. (Keep in mind that when the stand is

324
complete you will need to get back in the cars and make a U-turn that will
enable you to head back on Charles City Road. In any case, be cautious at
this intersection—many vehicles pass at high speed.)
Orientation: The route to our current location (Riddell’s Shop) is not on
the same path taken by Warren’s V Corps (the staff ride takes a more direct
route to save time). There was no settlement here during the war; the loca-
tion was named for a blacksmith’s shop nearby. Both sides had fought
in this area in 1862 in the Seven Day’s Battles. Warren deployed in this
vicinity to cover the movement of the other Union corps to the James. The
paths of the Charles City, Darbytown, and Willis Church Roads are the
same paths as in the Civil War. Controlling this crossroad prevented Lee
from probing east and discovering the Union move.
Description: Warren’s V Corps spent almost all of 13 June deployed at
this location. One cavalry brigade from Wilson’s division screened to the
west of the crossroads. Having fulfilled its mission, the V Corps departed
at 2000 for Charles City Courthouse.
     The Federal movements, to include Warren’s deployment here, helped
to keep Lee in the dark. Unable to take the initiative, Lee waited for signs
of Union intentions. Lee had his artillery bombard the Union lines at Cold
Harbor every night at 2100; each time the Federals responded and the
Confederate leader knew they were still in place. On the night of 12 June,
the Federal artillery response was noticeably weaker than normal. Even
so, on 13 June Lee sent Early and the II Corps (8,000 troops) to the Valley.
As Early was departing, Lee discovered that the Federals had left Cold
Harbor. Jefferson Davis suggested to Lee that he recall Early, but Lee
decided to let Early complete the move.
     After the discovery that the Union Army was not at Cold Harbor, Lee
tried to probe for the Federals. He ordered both of his remaining corps
(Anderson and Hill) across the Chickahominy toward Riddell’s Shop.
Confederate cavalry ran into the Union cavalry screen and pushed them
back. The Southerners halted in front of Warren’s infantry at Riddell’s
Shop at nightfall on 13 June. The Southerners occupied a line from White
Oak Swamp to Malvern Hill. Lee directed Hill to continue the advance the
next day.
     As Hill advanced early on 14 June, Lee discovered that the Federals
had left Riddell’s Shop. At 1210, Lee telegraphed Davis, “I think the
enemy must be preparing to move south of the James River” (as quoted
by Freeman, R.E. Lee, volume 3, 226-233, from Lee’s Dispatches:
Unpublished Letters of Robert E. Lee, C.S.A., to Jefferson Davis and the
War Department of the Confederate States of America, 1862-65, New


                                                                        325
York, NY: 1915, 227). Without his cavalry, Lee could not get a fix on
Grant’s moves, and he could not risk sending Confederate forces across
the James until he had more hard information on the Federals.
Vignettes: None.
Analysis: There are no specific points for analysis at this stand. You may
want to point out that Warren’s performance in the Overland Campaign
was uneven; however, he and the V Corps did an excellent job in screening
the army’s move at Riddell’s Shop.

                                                                                                 James River

                                                                        Map 64.

Directions: As mentioned earlier, you need to maneuver carefully at the
intersection of Charles City Road and Willis Church Road so that you
are back on Charles City Road heading east (opposite the direction you
traveled earlier). After 1.2 miles, you will come to an intersection. Keep
going straight—the road name will remain Charles City Road, but it will
change numbers from Route 156 to Route 600. After 4.4 miles, turn left on
Route 106 (Roxbury Road). Continue a short distance (0.2 mile) on Route
106 and then turn right on Route 609 (Barnett’s Road). After 3.7 miles
on Route 609, turn left on Route 602 (Lott Cary Road). Travel for 3.0
miles on Route 602 and then turn right on Route 618 (Adkins Road). After
4.5 miles you will come to a “T” intersection with Route 5 (John Tyler
Memorial Highway). Turn left at the “T” and then make an immediate
right turn (less than 0.1 mile) back on to Route 618 (Wilcox Wharf Road).
Continue on Route 618 until it ends at the James River where you will find
a parking lot at the landing. Park the cars in the lot and conduct the stand
on the riverbank where you can get a good view of the river.


328
Orientation: Using a map, show the students the location of the last stand
(Riddell’s Shop) and the path you drove to get here. You are currently at
Wilcox’s Landing. As you face the river, downriver is to the left; upriver
is to the right. Your current location is the landing where soldiers were fer-
ried across. The site where the Federals built their bridge should be visible
(in good weather) to the left (east). It is about 3 miles downriver at the
second bend in the James.
Description: Hancock’s II Corps arrived here (Wilcox’s Landing) at 1730
on 13 June. The troops began to embark on transports at 0900 the next day.
The II Corps’ crossing was completed by early morning on 15 June.
     At 1600 on 13 June, Union engineers, under Major James C. Duane
and Brigadier General Henry W. Benham, began construction on the James
River Bridge. They built the bridge from both ends, Weyanoke Neck on
the north bank and Windmill Point on the south. The bridge was completed
at 2300 on 13 June—it had taken only 7 hours to build. The bridge was
2,100 feet long and consisted of 101 pontoons and 3 schooners. It accom-
modated a four-foot tidal rise, and there was a swing span in the middle
that opened up for Federal ships moving to and from City Point.
     From 14 to 17 June, a major portion of the Army of the Potomac
crossed the bridge. The army’s trains, totaling 50 miles in length and
including 3,500 head of cattle, crossed at various times throughout all four
days. The IX Corps traversed on the evening of 15 June. Getty’s division
of the VI Corps crossed on 16 and 17 June. Finally, Wilson’s cavalry divi-
sion crossed on 17 June. The Federals dismantled the bridge the next day.
     The rest of the army crossed the James by various means. The XVIII
Corps reached Bermuda Hundred by boat on 14 June and marched on
Petersburg the next day. The II Corps ferried across the river from our
current location at Wilcox’s Landing on 14 and 15 June and later joined
Smith’s corps in the advance on Petersburg. The V Corps ferried across the
James on 16 June. Two divisions of the VI Corps embarked on ships near
the bridging site on 16 June and sailed to Bermuda Hundred.
     All told, by the end of 17 June, 100,000 Federal troops, 5,000 wagons,
56,000 horses and mules, and 3,500 cattle had crossed the James River
safely.
     In the meantime, Lee remained unaware of the Federal move and had
not shifted any of his troops south of the James. The gates to Petersburg
seemed wide open on 15 June as Beauregard with roughly 3,000 men faced
the advancing XVIII and II Corps, totaling over 30,000 men. It seemed
that the Confederates would not be able to hold the city, but fate would
dictate another outcome.


                                                                          329
Vignette: Horace Porter penned this account of Grant watching the cross-
ing of the James: “As the general-in-chief stood upon the bluff on the
north bank of the river on the morning of June 15, watching with unusual
interest the busy scene spread out before him, it presented a sight which
had never been equaled even in his extended experience in all the var-
ied phases of warfare. His cigar had been thrown aside, his hands were
clasped behind him, and he seemed lost in the contemplation of the spec-
tacle. The great bridge was the scene of a continuous movement of infan-
try columns, batteries of artillery, and wagon-trains. The approaches to the
river on both banks were covered with masses of troops moving briskly to
their positions or waiting patiently their turn to cross. . . . The bright sun,
shining through a clear sky upon the scene, cast its sheen upon the water,
was reflected from the burnished gun-barrels and glittering cannon, and
brought out with increased brilliancy the gay colors of the waving banners.
The calmly flowing river reflected the blue of the heavens, and mirrored
on its surface the beauties of nature that bordered it. The rich grain was
standing high in the surrounding fields. The harvest was almost ripe, but
the harvesters had fled. . . . It was a matchless pageant that could not fail
to inspire all beholders with the grandeur of achievement and the majesty
of military power. The man whose genius had conceived and whose skill
had executed this masterly movement stood watching the spectacle in pro-
found silence. Whether his mind was occupied with the contemplation
of its magnitude and success, or was busied with maturing plans for the
future, no one can tell. After a time, he woke from his reverie, mounted
his horse, and gave orders to have headquarters ferried across to the south
bank of the river.” (Porter, 199-200.)
Analysis:
1. Analyze the Federal crossing of the James. Why does it go so well
when other Federal moves in the past seemed so flawed?
2. Compare the James River crossing to river crossing operations today.
What aspects of a successful river crossing are the same today as in the
Civil War?

Directions: Depart Wilcox’s Landing heading north on Wilcox Wharf
Road. After 1.0 miles, turn left on Route 5 (John Tyler Memorial Highway)
heading west. Go for 7.1 miles on Route 5 and then turn left on Route 106
(also Route 156 and Roxbury Road—which changes its name to Jordan
Point Road). Continue south on Route 106, crossing over the James River.
After 4.0 miles, turn right on James River Drive (combined Route 106,
Route 156, and Route 10). Go 0.7 miles and turn left on Ruffin Road
(combined Route 106 and Route 156 Bypass). Continue on Ruffin Road
for 4.5 miles. You will come to the intersection with Prince George Drive.
Park at the gas station at the intersection and conduct the stand where you
can view the roads at the intersection.
Orientation: Re-orient the students to north, south, east, and west. Using
a map, remind them that we just left Wilcox’s Landing where Hancock’s

332
Corps made its crossing using ferryboats. Describe the road network to
the students. The one that we just came from, Ruffin Road (it becomes
Courthouse Road just past the intersection), was the main path of Hancock’s
II Corps and eventually goes to Prince George Court-House. The road that
turns to the right, Prince George Road, was the one on which Hancock
made his fateful turn.
Description: On 13 June at 1730, the II Corps arrived at Wilcox’s Landing
on the north side of the James River and spent most of the next day ferrying
across the river.
     Late in the evening on 14 June, Meade sent orders to Hancock. First,
Butler was sending 60,000 rations (three days’ worth) by river from
City Point to resupply the II Corps. As soon as the II Corps was issued
the rations, it was to go by “most direct route to Petersburg, taking up a
position where the City Point railroad crosses Harrison’s Creek. . . .” (OR,
series I, volume XL, part I, 303). These orders did not inform Hancock of
any assault on Petersburg.
     At 0400, Hancock sent a message to Seth Williams (Adjutant General,
Army of the Potomac) that all of the II Corps (except one regiment) was
on the south bank of the James, but they had not yet received the promised
rations. Two and a half hours later, Hancock sent another message to
Williams that the II Corps had still not received the rations.
     After another two and a half hours, Hancock decided not to wait. He
requested permission to move without the rations. Meade approved the
request, but the approval did not reach Hancock in a timely manner. First,
the signal station on the north side of the river did not deliver Meade’s
approval to Hancock’s request. Also, Lieutenant Colonel Morgan (the
II Corps Chief of Staff), who was at Meade’s headquarters when Meade
approved the II Corps move, was delayed in returning to his Corps
headquarters when his boat was grounded in the James River.
     Finally, at 1030, the move began (the rations had still not arrived). The
order of march was Birney’s Division in the lead, followed by Gibbon, and
then Barlow with the trains. Hancock and Morgan had a map provided by
Army headquarters. The map showed the supposed II Corps destination at
Harrison’s Creek at an incorrect location about 4 miles from Petersburg,
between that city and City Point. But Harrison’s Creek was not between
Petersburg and City Point—it was behind the Confederate lines. The map
was also inaccurate in its portrayal of the road network, and the Corps lost
time marching and countermarching. Eventually, Morgan found 2 African-
American guides to help get the Corps on a path toward Petersburg.
     By mid-afternoon, Hancock’s lead unit arrived at this position (the
intersection of Ruffin Road and Prince George Drive). Hancock had to

                                                                          333
make a choice at this crossroads—go straight or turn right. He ordered
Birney to turn right (north). This choice took the Corps toward Harrison’s
Creek as it incorrectly appeared on the Army map, i.e., near Old Court-
House. If Hancock had continued straight toward Prince George Court-
House, he would have arrived on Smith’s left flank in an excellent position
to support the XVIII Corps attack on Petersburg. But at this time (1500),
he was still unaware that his mission was to join in the assault. Birney’s
and Gibbon’s Divisions took the right-hand turn and marched toward Old
Court-House. Barlow’s Division and the II Corps trains were far enough in
the rear of the Corps column that they did not come to this crossroad; they
took a more northerly route. Eventually, Barlow’s troops and the trains got
lost. For the soldiers, the march route was exceedingly hot and dusty.
     Hancock, traveling with Gibbon’s division, was near the Old Court-
House by 1730. At this time a message arrived from Grant—it was
addressed to any division commander in the II Corps—indicating that he
was not able to find Meade and Hancock and was anxious enough to get
the Army of the Potomac to support Smith that he was sending directives
directly to division commanders. The message instructed the II Corps to
support Smith’s attack at Petersburg. This was the first order that Hancock
received that specified his mission as supporting an attack at Petersburg.
Coincidentally, just minutes later, one of Smith’s staff officers delivered
a message from the XVIII Corps commander. It urged Hancock to move
to Petersburg to help Smith’s attack. The II Corps column immediately
turned on a small road—the road that brought the corps to Petersburg from
Old Court-House and directly behind Smith’s Corps.
     At 1830, Birney reached the Bryant House on Bailey’s Creek, about
one mile behind Hink’s division of the XVIII Corps. Gibbon was right
behind Birney. Barlow and the II Corps trains took the City Point Road
(instead of the direct route from Old Court-House) and did not arrive until
daylight on 16 June. Thus, Hancock had two divisions at Petersburg as
darkness began to fall on 15 June. Although they had lost a lot of time
and it was late in the day, Hancock and Smith might have still attempted
an attack with the II Corps. Their decision not to attack is covered at the
next stand.
Vignette: Hancock stated that waiting for the rations was not the main
reason for the delay on 15 June. He placed more blame on the faulty map
and lack of a clear mission (to join Smith in the assault on Petersburg). He
wrote: “I spent the best hours of the day on the 15th in marching by an
incorrect map in search of a designated position, which, as described, was
not in existence or could not be found.” (OR, series I, volume XL, part I,
305.)
334
Analysis:
1. Who, if anyone is to blame for the II Corps delay? Is this Grant’s fault
for not coordinating the efforts of two separate armies (Butler’s Army of
the James and Meade’s Army of the Potomac)? Was Grant overconfident
and thought that Smith and Butler could take the city on their own?
2. Should Meade be blamed for not giving a more specific mission
to Hancock, and not taking control of the fight for Petersburg (Meade
remained at the James River crossing site throughout 15 June)? What
errors, if any, did Hancock commit?
3. In fact, is no one to blame—were the Federal difficulties normal
“friction of war” or simply bad luck?
4. Was the apparently sloppy Union staff work another sign of the decay of
the Army’s effectiveness—the wear of a month of continual campaigning?
Or perhaps, did the Union staffs and leaders get so wrapped up in the move
to the James that they failed to think of operations after they had crossed
the river?

Directions: Note that the path described here is not the shortest route to
Battery 5, but it allows you to follow Hancock’s historical route. From

Street when the road splits, and then back to Oaklawn Boulevard when the
roads come together again). After 4.4 miles, take the exit to the right for
the Petersburg National Military Park. After going a short distance, park
in the NPS parking lot at the park headquarters (note that you will have to
pay an entrance fee for the park at a gate in the entrance to the headquar-
ters area). After parking the vehicles, proceed down the walking path that
leads to Battery 5 (or Redoubt 5). The stand will be done in several loca-
tions, the first of which is in the battery itself.
Orientation: You have just come from Hancock’s turn (show the location
on the map). You are currently located at Battery 5 where “Baldy” Smith’s

336
XVIII Corps troops broke through and captured a portion of the Dimmock
Line on 15 June 1864.
     The battery is somewhat different in shape than at the time of the
Union assault. Originally the battery was an open-back structure with its
walls facing mainly northeast and northwest. After the Federals took the
battery, they built a wall across the open rear of the redoubt and incorpo-
rated it into the Federal lines surrounding the city.
     The roadbed of what was the City Point Railroad is to the left rear
(northwest) of the battery (you might be able to view this roadbed better
at the second part of the stand). There are no remains of Battery 6, which
was to the southeast of your location. It would have been located near
some trees on the east side of the parking lot. Note that the entrenched bat-
teries of the Confederate lines were connected by trenches. Most of these
trenches do not currently exist, but the NPS sometimes cuts the grass in
a pattern in which the line of trenches shows as higher grass. A sample of
this should be visible leading out of Battery 5 toward Battery 6.
     The stand will be done in four parts and four locations. First, you will
set the Confederate defense from Battery 5. Second, walk down the path
leading out the north end of the battery and stop where you can see the low
ground where the City Point Railroad ran. Here you will discuss Butler’s
earlier efforts to take Petersburg. Third, continue on the walk path to the
large mortar called the Dictator and tell the story of this unique weapon.
Finally, continue on the path until you emerge back near Battery 5. Here
you will cover the Federal attack on 15 June.

Description: The city of Petersburg was originally fortified in the summer
of 1862. The fortifications were designed by Captain Charles Dimmock
and became known as the “Dimmock Line.” The line of works stretched
10 miles on the east, south, and west of the city, and its flanks rested on
the Appomattox River. On completion, the line included 55 numbered
artillery battery positions connected by infantry parapets. The forward
approaches were covered by ditches 8 feet deep and 15 feet wide and a
series of various entanglements (to include abatis and cheveaux de fraise).
Various commanders, to include Beauregard, estimated that it would take
a 20,000-man garrison to adequately man the line. When the war came
to Petersburg in the spring of 1864, the line was in some disrepair, which
the Confederates attempted to correct with only partial success. Battery 5
itself contained four artillery pieces with crews (about 40 men).
     (Move to the second location on the walk path north of the battery.)
     After his repulse at Drewry’s Bluff in mid-May, Butler had become
interested in Petersburg. Contrary to Grant’s comment, Butler was not


                                                                         337
“bottled up” on Bermuda Hundred and had the option, among others, to
advance on Petersburg. Prior to the 15 June attack by the XVIII Corps,
Butler planned and attempted to launch three offensive movements on the
city. The first was intended for 29 May, but it was canceled when Smith’s
corps was suddenly sent to Grant at Cold Harbor. The second was planned
for 2 June, but a Confederate probe launched by Beauregard scuttled that
effort as well.
     The third expedition was launched on 9 June. Quincy Gillmore, com-
mander of the X Corps, was selected by Butler to lead the effort. Gillmore
was given two infantry brigades under Colonel Joseph R. Hawley and
Brigadier General Edward W. Hinks as well as Brigadier General August
Kautz’s small cavalry division. The mission was to enter Petersburg and
burn bridges—not to occupy the city.
     On 9 June, Petersburg’s Confederate garrison was very weak.
Beauregard was down to 5,500 troops to defend both Bermuda Hundred
and Petersburg. Of these, about 1,200 men were at Petersburg. The
Petersburg garrison consisted only of one veteran infantry regiment—the
46th Virginia, one company of the 23d South Carolina, and two battalions
of city militia.
     On the morning of 9 June, about 7,900 troops under Gilmore approached
the city in three columns: Hawley’s brigade along the City Point (River)
Road; Hinks’ brigade of United States Colored Troops (USCT) along the
Jordan Point Road; and the cavalry along the Jerusalem Plank Road. The
fighting began at about 0900, and by 1030, Hawley’s Brigade was stopped
at Battery 5. Likewise, Hinks’ brigade was stopped by a heavy crossfire
from some militia and the 46th Virginia Regiment near Battery 9. At 1315,
however, Kautz’s troopers overran the militia defending at Battery 27 on
the Plank Road and moved to enter the city. Kautz’s advance was stopped,
however, by John Dearing’s cavalry and Graham’s battery on reservoir
hill. By 1530, all of the Federals had withdrawn. (See vignettes for a
humorous encounter between Butler and a Confederate prisoner from the
9 June fight.)
     The action had several interesting results. The Federals lost 52 killed,
wounded, and missing. The Confederate losses were 150 killed, wounded,
and missing. Butler relieved Gillmore, but perhaps the most important
result was that Beauregard realized that Petersburg’s defenses were criti-
cally weak, and he reinforced the garrison with a brigade, bringing the
total number of defenders to 2,200 men instead of 1,200 men.
     (Move to the Dictator location.)
     This huge mortar was cast by Mr. Carles Knapp, at his well-known iron
works in Pittsburg, Pennsylvania. The weapon was used in the summer of

338
1864, during the siege operations against Petersburg. It weighed 17,120
pounds and was transported from City Point on a railway car (truck) along
the City Point and Petersburg Railroad and then along a specially built
spur line to this location. The truck was strong enough to function as the
platform for the mortar.
     The Dictator was a 13-inch mortar, firing a shell weighing 200 pounds,
with a maximum charge of 20 pounds of powder. At an angle of elevation
of 45 degrees, the range of the weapon was 4,235 yards. It was alleged that
one round reached Centre Hill in Petersburg, and thus this round would
have traveled at least 2.7 miles or 4,752 yards. The mortar and platform
moved on a curved rail track to be aimed for deflection. The normal charge
of 14 pounds of powder caused a recoil on the carriage of 2 feet and a
recoil on the car of 12 feet.
     In addition to the nickname of the Dictator, it was also called the
Petersburg Express. Its main targets were the Chesterfield Battery across
the Appomattox River and the city of Petersburg itself. The weapon on
display is a replica (the original was most likely scrapped soon after the
war).
     (Move to the final location near the battery.)
     After the action on 9 June, Beauregard redoubled his efforts to get
reinforcements from Davis and Lee. Davis, in essence, ignored him. Lee
was still unsure of Grant’s intent and hesitated sending aid to Beauregard
at Petersburg until he knew what Grant would do next. Additionally, on
12 June, Lee had sent Early’s II Corps to the Shenandoah Valley to stop
David Hunter’s advance up the Shenandoah Valley and the destruction of
Lee’s logistics source there; thus Lee had less troops to spare.
     Lee discovered the Union withdrawal from Cold Harbor on 13 June,
but merely saw it as another shallow left hook by the Federals and did
not suspect Grant would try to make a jump across the James River south
of Richmond. Based on these assumptions, Lee made no major moves
on 13 and 14 June. On the evening of 14 June, Beauregard identified the
return of “Baldy” Smith’s XVIII Corps to his front and reported this to
Lee, but the Confederate Army commander still did not respond.
     At 1130 on 15 June, as Smith’s 15,000 Federals approached Petersburg,
Lee finally released Hoke’s Division to Beauregard. But the division had
to travel 18 miles to get to Petersburg. Until Hoke’s Division could reach
Petersburg that night, the city was held by only one veteran infantry bri-
gade (Wise’s), some reserves, and Dearing’s cavalry.
     In the mean time, Smith’s XVIII Corps returned to Bermuda Hundred
from its trek to Cold Harbor on the evening of 14–15 June. The corps
had moved from White House on the York, down that river, then up the
                                                                       339
James to Bermuda Hundred, and disembarked there. At sunset on 14
June, Smith received his orders to attack Petersburg on the morning of
15 June. In addition to his own divisions, depleted at Cold Harbor, Smith
was to receive Hinks’ United States Colored Troops (USCT) Division and
Kautz’s cavalry division, which had to link up and perform their respec-
tive missions en route.
     After some confusion disembarking his troops at both Bermuda
Hundred and Point of Rocks, Smith moved on the city the morning of
15 June. Effective delaying actions by the Confederates combined with
caution among the Union commanders meant that the march from the
landing to the outskirts of Petersburg—about 5 miles—took six hours
(0500 to 1100). Union units then took another three hours to get into battle
formations arrayed around the Dimmock Line.
     As he gazed at the Dimmock Line, Smith was awed by the appear-
ance of the formidable works. His previous experience attacking works at
Cold Harbor now gave him pause. As a result, he held his troops in place
until he could conduct a reconnaissance of the enemy positions, looking
for a weak point. Smith, lacking a staff engineer, took from 1300 to 1500
to analyze the Dimmock Line from Battery 1 to Battery 9 (Smith himself
was an engineer and known to be very meticulous).
     Smith formulated his plan and rode all the way to his right flank to
explain his concept personally to Brigadier General John H. Martindale,
one of his division commanders. Then Smith returned to his center divi-
sion, under Major General W.T.H. Brooks, and made final preparations for
the attack. The plan was basically for his three divisions to attack on line.
Martindale’s division was to attack on the right, Brooks in the center, and
Hinks on the left. Smith also decided that the best way to attack the sub-
stantial, but lightly held, entrenchments was to advance in heavy skirmish
lines rather than traditional regimental lines or heavy assault columns that
would be more vulnerable to artillery fire. It was now 1700.
     Amazingly, there was one further delay. Smith’s chief of artillery for
this operation, Captain Frederick Follett, had sent the artillery horses to
the rear for watering, and it took two more hours to get them back and shift
the artillery into positions to support the attack. While making his prepara-
tions, at about 1600, Smith learned that Hancock’s II Corps was across the
James River, and Grant gave Smith authority to coordinate with Hancock
to join the attack. But Hancock did not begin to arrive until 1830.
     Baldy Smith’s Federals finally launched their assault at about 1900.
Colonel Louis Bell’s Brigade (attached to Brooks’ Division) made the ini-
tial penetration between Batteries 5 and 6, making use of a ravine that


340
covered their advance. At almost the same time, the 13th New Hampshire
Regiment (Burnham’s Brigade, Brook’s Division) stormed the face of
Battery 5. Under pressure from their front, right, and rear (Bell’s men), the
defenders of Battery 5 surrendered.
     Almost immediately after the fall of Battery 5, Hinks’ African-
American Division attacked on Brooks’ left. Assisted by some of Bell’s
troops, Hinks’ men captured Battery 6. The loss of these two Batteries (5
and 6) began to unhinge adjacent portions of the Dimmock Line. Hinks’
soldiers quickly took Battery 7, and then—as more of the Black troops
were committed further south—they took Batteries 8 and 9. Eventually,
Hinks’ Division was able to gain Batteries 10 and 11 before the Union
attack ran out of steam. On the other flank, Battery 4 fell relatively quickly,
and then after a tougher battle, Martindale’s men captured Battery 3. All
told, Smith’s Corps had gained 3½ miles of Confederate lines (Batteries
3 through 11).
     The Federals suffered 1,300 killed, 7,500 wounded, and 1,800 miss-
ing for a total of 10,600 losses in the assault. Confederate losses were
estimated at 4,000 total killed, wounded, and missing.
     Despite the losses, and even after all of the delays and mistakes on the
Union side, they appeared to have victory in their grasp on the evening of
15 June. Hancock’s lead troops had begun to arrive just as Smith’s men
were attacking, but it would be dark by the time all units of Hancock’s
two available divisions were in place. Hancock was senior to Smith, but
he yielded to Smith’s judgment as the commander most familiar with the
situation on the spot. Smith requested Hancock to relieve several of the
XVIII Corps units of their captured positions and decided against any fur-
ther attacks.
     Smith may have been discouraged from further action by the com-
ing nightfall or the exhaustion of his own Corps. Perhaps more revealing
was Smith’s dispatch to Butler, which reported, “It is impossible for me
to go further tonight, but, unless I misapprehend the topography, I hold
the key to Petersburg.” (OR, series I, volume XL, part I, 83). Beauregard
knew he was in a desperate situation, but also knew that Smith needed to
take advantage of the opportunity: “Strange to say, General Smith con-
tented himself with breaking into our lines, and attempted nothing further
that night. . . . Petersburg at that hour was clearly at the mercy of the
Federal commander, who had all but captured it, and only failed of final
success because he could not realize the fact of the unparalleled dispar-
ity between the two contending forces.” (P.G.T. Beauregard, “Four Days
of Battle at Gettysburg,” from Battles and Leaders of the Civil War The


                                                                           341
Way to Appomattox, volume 4, edited by Robert Underwood Johnson and
Clarence Clough Buel, New York, NY: Castle Books, 1956, 541). (See
vignettes for one soldier’s view of the decision not to attack.)
    During the night, Beauregard built new defensive positions behind
the lines he had lost. For the next three days (16 to 18 June), the Union
Army hammered at the Confederate defenses, took some more positions,
but failed to take the city. Petersburg, which seemed to be in the Union
grasp on 15 June 1864, would take another 9 months to fall.
Vignettes:
1. On 9 June, after the Confederate prisoners (of the city’s militia) cap-
tured at Battery 27 were brought by Kautz’s cavalrymen into Bermuda
Hundred, Butler demanded to see them for interrogation. The first man the
general interviewed was Anthony Keiley, a Petersburg lawyer. When he
was asked about the strength of the troops defending Battery 27, Keiley
honestly replied with the answer. However, when asked about the strength
of the city’s garrison, Keiley declined to say. Butler chided Keiley by say-
ing that he already knew there were few soldiers in the town. Keiley was
somewhat amazed at this and asked Butler how he could possibly know,
to which Butler dryly replied: “By this infallible induction: if there was a
soldier in town, no lawyer would get into the trenches!” (William Glenn
Robertson, The Petersburg Campaign: The Battle of Old Men and Young
Boys June 9, 1864, Lynchburg, VA, 1989, 85.)
2. A young soldier, George Ulmer, from a Maine regiment in Smith’s
XVIII Corps did not agree with Smith’s decision to suspend attacks on
the evening of 15 June. He later wrote: “I swore all night. I kicked and
condemned every general there was in the army for the blunder I saw they
were making. I only wished I could be the commanding general for one
hour. But it was no use; I couldn’t be.” (Noah Andre Trudeau, The Last
Citadel, Petersburg, Virginia, June 1864–April 1865, Baton Rouge, LA:
Louisiana State University Press, 1991, 41.)
Analysis:
1. Why do the Federals fail to take Petersburg on 15 June? Does the
blame fall mainly on Smith’s shoulders? Why or why not? Do Grant or
Meade deserve most of the blame for failing to coordinate additional
forces (Hancock) for the attack and for being absent from the field? Was it
just bad luck?
2. Assess the Confederate leadership in defending Petersburg. Why is
Beauregard so successful with so few resources? Lee continued to be slow


342
to react to Grant’s move south of the James; should he have done more to
aid Beauregard? Why or why not?
3. Despite the failure to take Petersburg in mid-June, was Grant’s overall
shift to Petersburg a success? Was it a major step toward winning the war,
or did Grant plunge the Army of the Potomac into a lengthy siege that
prolonged the war?




                                                                      343
                         IV. Integration Phase
Introduction
     As this handbook has previously emphasized, a staff ride consists of
three phases. The first phase is the “Preliminary Study Phase.” This phase
is conducted before the visit to the battlefield and prepares the students
for the visit. The second phase is the “Field Study Phase.” This phase is
conducted on the battlefield and enables students to understand historical
events through analysis of the actual terrain. The final phase of a staff ride
is the “Integration Phase.” No staff ride is complete without an integration
phase, because it is critical for the students to understand what happened,
why it happened, and, most importantly, what can be learned from the
study of the battle or campaign.
     There are several factors that the staff ride leader should consider
when planning for and conducting the integration phase. First, the leader
must work with the organization that is participating in the ride and select
a time and location for the integration session. Occasionally, units may
have to depart shortly after the last stand of the field phase, and the staff
ride leader must conduct the integration phase on the battlefield imme-
diately after completing the field study phase. However, when possible,
students should have some time for personal reflection and thought before
the integration phase. Thus, the integration phase is best if conducted the
day after the field study phase ends. Even if you cannot wait an extra day,
it is best to do the integration session at a location different from the last
stand, a place comfortable and dry that will encourage open discussion
from all the participants.
     The staff ride leader should organize the integration phase based on
the unit, time available, and training objectives. The leader can conduct
the integration phase in a format similar to an after action review (AAR),
or may simply lead a discussion with participants on what they learned.
You can have specific students brief particular items, or just have an
open discussion with minimal structure. It is important to keep in mind
that the integration phase is not an AAR of the ride itself (i.e., ways to
improve the ride). While it is useful to seek constructive criticism in order
to continue to improve the ride, this should be done at another time or
perhaps with written AAR comments. Instead, the integration phase is
used for the students of the campaign to integrate their preliminary study
with the fieldwork to gain insights that are relevant to their current duties
and enhance their professional development. Whatever method the staff
ride leader chooses to employ, the most important thing to remember is
that the participants should do the majority of the talking.
                                                                          345
    One method that often produces a fruitful integration phase is to con-
duct the session in three parts based on three broad questions. Sometimes,
the leader need only present the general question and let others carry the
conversation, or the leader may have to ask more follow-up questions to
prod the discussion. Each of the three questions is discussed below.
What aspects of the campaign had you developed in the preliminary
study phase that changed or were strongly reinforced because of your
study of the ground?
     This is a crucial question because seeing the terrain is central to a staff
ride, otherwise the campaign could simply be studied in the classroom.
Of course, students may develop a wide range of answers based on
personal study and observations in the field. Some of the more popular
aspects of the discussion of terrain for the Overland Campaign include
the vast distances of the operational maneuver, the wooded nature of
the Wilderness, Upton’s use of cover and concealment in his attack, the
limited space of the Bloody Angle (so many men tragically died in such
a confined area), the effectiveness of Lee’s inverted “V” position on the
North Anna, the depth of the defenses at Cold Harbor, and the width of
the James River that needed to be bridged. The staff ride leader can ask
a related question, which may also generate good discussion: Did seeing
the terrain alter your opinion of any of the leaders? A common response
to this question is that Grant may not deserve the label of “butcher” given
the weapons systems of the day and the defensive advantages of the terrain
and field fortifications.
What aspects of warfare have changed and what aspects have remained
the same since the Overland Campaign?
      The answers to the “changed” aspects will probably seem more
obvious to the modern military professional and often will be related to
technology. This may include changes in weapons, transportation systems,
communications, and numerous other pieces of equipment. The aspects
that have “remained the same” may not seem as numerous at first, but
the students will often build on some initial answers and find many good
items. The role of personalities; command relationships; the importance of
logistics; the need for strong, positive leadership and an ability to motivate
soldiers; the importance of operational maneuver; determination; courage;
and fear are just some of the items of warfare that seem to have changed
little since 1864. Depending on the group, you may want to ask a few
more focused questions. For example, if you have a quartermaster unit,
you can ask the following: What aspects of logistics have changed and
what aspects have remained the same?

346
What insights can the modern military professional gain from the
Overland Campaign that are relevant today?
     Clearly, the participants can take this discussion into a vast number
of arenas. Once again, the type of unit participating in the staff ride might
help to guide the discussion. For example, a military intelligence unit
might focus the commander’s situational awareness, intelligence gather-
ing, and the importance of reconnaissance. Keeping in mind that the Over-
land Campaign is as much an operational level staff ride as it is tactical, it
might be useful to prompt discussion by using the elements of operational
design as a framework for relevant lessons. These elements are:
          End state/military conditions.
          Center of gravity.
          Decisive points and objectives.
          Lines of operations.
          Culmination point.
          Operational reach/approach/pause.
          Simultaneous and sequential operations.
          Tempo.
     These terms are provided as a tool; the staff ride leader may use some
of them, use another framework, or simply let the students take the discus-
sion in whatever direction they want.
     The three suggested integration phase questions are to aid in sparking
discussion, not to provide hard and fast “rules” of warfare. Note that the
handbook provides examples of possible answers to the questions, but it
does not attempt to provide a list of “right” answers. The staff ride leader
should take time before the session to write down his or her own answers
to these questions to have some potential ideas to generate student discus-
sion. At the same time, the staff ride leader should strive for the partici-
pants to develop their own answers, and thus be prepared to let the discus-
sion roam many different paths.

2. Logistics.
     a. Meals. There are many restaurants in Fredericksburg, Richmond,
and Ashland that are convenient to hotel locations and should take care
of breakfast and dinner. Lunch can either be a box lunch carried on the
vehicles or you can eat at nearby fast-food restaurants. As noted in the
stands, we have recommended times to pause in the staff ride for lunch on
all three days.
    b. Lodging. Groups can find many hotels in Fredericksburg (for the
night after day 1) and in either Ashland or Richmond (for the night after
day 2). If the group wants to cut down on lodging costs, there are many
military bases in Virginia and the Washington, DC, area, but they are not
as conveniently located as the hotels.
    c. Travel. If the group is flying to the area, the Richmond airport is
the most convenient to use. Once on the ground, larger groups will need
to contract for a bus—make sure it has a microphone and public address
system as well as a restroom. Smaller groups (less than 20) might find it
easier for parking and maneuvering to use rental vans.
3. Other considerations.
    a. A reconnaissance of the stands and route just prior to execution of
the ride is imperative for a successful staff ride.
    b. Ensure that every member of the group has water. Additionally,
some restrooms are available on the route. Plan for adequate stops at these
facilities.
    c. Ensure that your group has proper clothing for inclement weather.
Thunderstorms can occur in any season. Some walking is required for each
of the major battlefields you visit. Comfortable boots or hiking shoes are
recommended. We recommend that you do not wear sandals or running
shoes.
    d. Mosquitoes, ants, chiggers, ticks, and other insects are prevalent
from March to October, so insect repellent is advised. Poison ivy is also
present in some of the more remote areas.
    e. Road traffic in the Wilderness areas can be heavy. The area has
several nearby housing subdivisions that ensure almost constant traffic
along the Orange Turnpike (Virginia Highway 20), the Orange Plank
Road (County Road 621), and Brock Road (County Road 613). Several

                                                                       351
stands are conducted near major roads and some foot movement across or
parallel to the roads is necessary. Be sure to use traffic guards and stress
safety to group members when getting off and on the vehicles and when
moving across or near the roads. Similarly, be careful of US Highway 1
and the highly traveled roads around Richmond.
